Estimate directed transfer entropy between categorical sequences

Source: R/transfer_entropy.R
transfer_entropy.Rd

transfer_entropy() (experimental) estimates directed transfer entropy between categorical sequences. Transfer entropy (Schreiber, 2000) measures directed predictive information: how much knowing the past of a source series reduces uncertainty about the future of a target series, beyond what the target's own past already tells. Because it conditions on the target's history, it is not inflated when a state merely tends to persist, which inflates lagged association measures for processes with strong momentum. Transfer entropy is unsigned: a large value means strong directed dependence, which may make the target more or less likely. Read it alongside the signed residuals and Yule's Q of transitions().

It works in two modes. With one set of sequences (y = NULL), it treats each state as an indicator series (in the state or not) and returns the transfer entropy from every state to every other state, a directed information-flow network among the states. With very few states the indicator series of the other states carry nearly the same information, so several pairs can share a value; the bivariate mode avoids this. With two aligned sets of sequences (x and y), it returns the transfer entropy between the two series in both directions, using their full alphabets.

Transfer entropy is in bits. The surrogate test (default) shuffles the source to build a null distribution, which gives a p-value and an effective transfer entropy with the average surrogate value subtracted. For the classical test of sequential dependence use lsa().

Usage

transfer_entropy(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  lag = 1L,
  history = 1L,
  test = c("surrogate", "none"),
  R = 199L,
  normalize = TRUE,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

x

Categorical sequences: a vector (one sequence) or a matrix or data frame with one sequence per row and one time point per column, padded with NA, as accepted by lsa().

y

Optional second set of sequences of the same shape as x, for the bivariate mode. Default NULL (state-flow network of x).

lag

Prediction horizon, an integer of at least 1 (default 1).

history

Number of past steps of the target conditioned on, an integer of at least 1 (default 1).

test

"surrogate" (default) for the surrogate test, or "none".

R

Number of surrogates (default 199).

normalize

Add te_normalised, transfer entropy as a share of the target's remaining uncertainty given its own history, in [0, 1] (default TRUE).

seed

Optional seed for the surrogate test (default NULL). The session's random number state is restored on exit.

Value

A data.frame with one row per ordered pair (from, to) and the columns te (bits), te_effective (with test = "surrogate"), te_normalised (with normalize = TRUE), p (with test = "surrogate") and n (number of transitions used), sorted by decreasing te. In the state-flow mode there is one row per ordered pair of distinct states; in the bivariate mode two rows, named after the arguments.

Conditions

Errors carry the class lagdynamics_error and lagdynamics_bad_input when lag, history or R is not a positive whole number, or when x and y are not aligned (different numbers of sequences or different lengths within a sequence).

References

Schreiber, T. (2000). Measuring information transfer. Physical Review Letters, 85(2), 461-464.

See also

lsa(), transitions(), lsa_lags()

Examples

# Information flow among the engagement states
transfer_entropy(engagement, test = "none")
#>         from         to          te te_normalised    n
#> 1     Active Disengaged 0.036448215   0.060023389 1734
#> 2    Average Disengaged 0.036448215   0.060023389 1734
#> 3     Active    Average 0.006949150   0.007517345 1734
#> 4 Disengaged    Average 0.006949150   0.007517345 1734
#> 5    Average     Active 0.004793199   0.006345037 1734
#> 6 Disengaged     Active 0.004793199   0.006345037 1734

# With the surrogate test (an analysis would use more surrogates)
transfer_entropy(engagement, R = 19, seed = 1)
#>         from         to          te te_effective te_normalised    p    n
#> 1     Active Disengaged 0.036448215  0.035496615   0.060023389 0.05 1734
#> 2    Average Disengaged 0.036448215  0.035862001   0.060023389 0.05 1734
#> 3     Active    Average 0.006949150  0.005764179   0.007517345 0.05 1734
#> 4 Disengaged    Average 0.006949150  0.005940226   0.007517345 0.05 1734
#> 5    Average     Active 0.004793199  0.003806708   0.006345037 0.05 1734
#> 6 Disengaged     Active 0.004793199  0.004268635   0.006345037 0.05 1734

# Between two aligned series
mood <- c("calm", "calm", "tense", "tense", "calm", "tense", "tense", "calm")
effort <- c("low", "low", "low", "high", "high", "low", "high", "high")
transfer_entropy(mood, effort, test = "none")
#>     from     to        te te_normalised n
#> 1   mood effort 0.9649839     1.0000000 7
#> 2 effort   mood 0.6792696     0.7039181 7
